paragraphs.text: Anthropic has told prospective investors that it has met one of the key thresholds in its own safety framework. In the second amendment to its IPO prospectus, dated November 10, 2026, the company wrote that it made a determination that it has met the threshold for dramatically accelerated AI progress, according to Yahoo Finance and to Alex Wilhelm's Cautious Optimism newsletter.

The determination rests on what Anthropic expects from future models and on its overall rate of progress, not on an observed capability of a current model, both outlets reported. Yahoo Finance noted that crossing the line triggers more safeguards rather than a shutdown, and that Anthropic said it is still weighing what the result means.

Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy sets out capability levels that require stronger protections. One of them concerns automated AI research. As quoted by Cautious Optimism, it is met if Anthropic determines that its models could fully substitute for its research scientists and engineers at competitive cost, or that AI progress has sharply accelerated in a way likely tied to automating AI research. Yahoo Finance and CellCog describe that acceleration as roughly two years of progress, at the 2018 to 2024 pace, compressed into one year.

Outside evidence points the same way. Yahoo Finance reported that METR, an independent AI testing nonprofit, estimated Anthropic's models have improved about 1.9 times as fast since October 2025 as before. A separate METR review called Anthropic's August argument that it remained below the threshold overstated and said a crossing was plausible by mid-July.
How the wording changed across three filings

The language moved quickly. Cautious Optimism reported that the original S-1 of October 26 warned that Anthropic might not identify a significant acceleration until after it had happened. The first amendment, filed November 2, said its estimates suggested it may imminently meet the threshold and stated that no current model had been designated as exceeding it. The second amendment, eight days later, dropped that sentence and said the threshold had been met, according to CellCog's comparison of the documents.

The newer filing also adds context on control. Yahoo Finance reported that Anthropic said it does not expect to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build later generations of frontier models without meaningful human oversight, and that it is weighing policy changes to keep humans in control. The filing also warns that as Claude speeds up work inside the company, Anthropic may lose visibility into some processes in ways that are hard for people to understand and control.

The disclosure arrives days before the listing. Yahoo Finance reported a price range of $70 to $78 per share, which values the company at up to about $1.4 trillion on a fully diluted basis, with trading possible as soon as November 19. Nvidia and Google are each buying $10 billion of stock at the IPO price as part of a $26 billion private placement, the outlet said.

The filing turns a safety framework that used to be discussed mainly in policy circles into a disclosure that public market investors will read. It is also a rare case of an AI developer stating in a legal document, rather than in a blog post or interview, that its own systems are speeding up its research. Because the determination rests on expectations about future models, the concrete safeguards Anthropic adopts in response will say more about its practical meaning than the threshold itself.

Anthropic has said it will publish further reports on the implications. The next signal is whether those reports, or later prospectus changes before trading begins, spell out specific new safeguards such as human approval of research decisions.
